title: Why You'd Never Want to Swim on Titan
screen_title: Why You'd Never Want to Swim on Titan
subtitle: Saturn's giant moon, where it rains gasoline-like methane
yt_title: Why You'd Never Want to Swim on Titan
intro: What would happen if you stood on Titan, Saturn's giant moon? We drop through an orange haze thicker than Earth's air, walk on ice as hard as rock, watch giant raindrops of methane drift down in slow motion, and find out what would happen if you tried to swim in its seas. Stay to the end to find out how, on Titan, you could fly with your own arms.

Would you strap on wings and fly on Titan?

segments.text: What if you jumped into a lake on Titan? You'd sink like a stone. The liquid would boil against your skin, and then you'd freeze solid. But up in the sky, you could fly like a bird. How?

files: Titan in true color by Kevin M. Gill.jpg
visual.query: Titan in true color by Kevin M. Gill

segments.text: Welcome to Next Stop: Universe. If you enjoy calm, easy-to-follow journeys through space, tap subscribe. Today we land on the strangest moon in the solar system. So, let's go.

files: Good Morning From the International Space Station.jpg
visual.query: Good Morning From the International Space Station

segments.text: This is Titan. The largest moon of Saturn. It's bigger than the planet Mercury.

files: Titan in true color by Kevin M. Gill.jpg
visual.query: Titan in true color by Kevin M. Gill

segments.headline: Saturn's giant moon

segments.text: And it's the only moon in the solar system with a thick atmosphere. It has clouds, rain, rivers, lakes and seas. It's the only other world we know where liquid falls from the sky and flows across the ground.
segments.headline: Rain, rivers and seas

segments.text: It sounds like Earth. But every single part of it would kill you in its own strange way. And stay to the end, because on Titan, you could do something no human can do on Earth. You could fly, using your own arms.
segments.headline: Fly like a bird?

segments.text: First, getting there. Titan orbits Saturn, about one point four billion kilometers from Earth. Even a radio signal takes well over an hour to make the trip.

visual.label: for a radio signal to reach Titan

segments.text: The Cassini spacecraft took almost seven years to get there. It carried a small passenger, a probe called Huygens, built by the European Space Agency.
segments.headline: Cassini and Huygens

segments.text: As you arrive, Saturn fills the sky, with its rings stretched out like a bright blade. But Titan itself is just a fuzzy orange ball. You can't see the ground at all.

files: Saturn global view from Cassini, rings open Better Colour.png
visual.query: Saturn global view from Cassini, rings open Better Colour

segments.headline: Arriving at Saturn

segments.text: So we dive in. Titan's atmosphere is enormous. It reaches about ten times higher than Earth's.
segments.headline: A giant atmosphere

segments.text: It's mostly nitrogen, like the air you're breathing right now. But it's mixed with methane, the gas in a kitchen stove. Sunlight breaks the methane apart, and the pieces join into a thick, orange smog.

files: Titan in true color by Kevin M. Gill.jpg
visual.query: Titan in true color by Kevin M. Gill

segments.headline: An orange smog

segments.text: As you fall, the sky glows orange all around you. Like falling through a sunset that never ends.
On January fourteenth, 2005, Huygens made this same fall. It drifted down under parachutes for about two and a half hours.

visual.label: Huygens lands on Titan
visual.sub: the most distant landing ever made

segments.text: It's still the most distant landing ever made. And this is what it saw on the ground.
segments.headline: The view from the ground

segments.text: Huygens hit the ground at about the speed of a dropped ball, and kept sending pictures and measurements for about seventy-two minutes, until Cassini flew out of range. The ground felt a bit like damp sand, with a thin frozen crust on top.

visual.label: Huygens kept talking from the surface

segments.text: Those round stones look like river pebbles. And that's exactly what they are. But they aren't made of rock. They're made of water ice, frozen as hard as granite.
segments.headline: Pebbles of ice

segments.text: It's minus one hundred seventy-nine degrees Celsius on the ground. Cold enough to freeze the air in your lungs, if you could even breathe it.
Here's the surprise. The air pressure is only about one and a half times Earth's. You wouldn't be crushed. On Titan, you wouldn't need a pressure suit at all.
You would need a heated suit and an oxygen mask. There's no oxygen to breathe. And the cold would pull the heat from your body in minutes.

files: Ed White First American Spacewalker - GPN-2000-001180.jpg
visual.query: Ed White First American Spacewalker - GPN-2000-001180

segments.headline: Mask and heated suit

segments.text: It's also dark. Sunlight on Titan is about a hundred times weaker than on Earth, and the haze swallows most of it. Noon on Titan looks like a dim evening at home.

files: Snowfall at night over Brofjorden and Preemraff oil refinery.jpg
visual.query: Snowfall at night over Brofjorden and Preemraff oil refinery

segments.headline: Noon looks like dusk

segments.text: Quick question for you. Did you know Titan is bigger than the planet Mercury? Tell us in the comments.

visual.q: Did you know Titan is bigger than the planet Mercury?

segments.text: Now let's spend a day here. And a day on Titan is long. Titan always keeps the same face toward Saturn, so one day lasts as long as one orbit. Almost sixteen Earth days.

From the side facing Saturn, the giant planet hangs in the sky and never moves. It would look enormous, about ten times wider than our full Moon. But the orange haze hides it almost completely. You'd stand under the most spectacular view in the solar system, and see nothing.

files: Backlit Saturn from Cassini Orbiter 2007 May 9.jpg
visual.query: Backlit Saturn from Cassini Orbiter 2007 May 9

segments.headline: Saturn, hidden

segments.text: Near the equator, you'd find huge dunes, taller than a thirty-story building, stretching for hundreds of kilometers. But the sand isn't rock. It's made of dark grains of frozen hydrocarbons, a bit like coffee grounds.
segments.headline: Dunes of dark grains

segments.text: And the seasons are slow. Saturn takes about twenty-nine years to circle the Sun, so each season on Titan lasts about seven years. Summer storms near the lakes are rare, and wonderful to watch.
Now the weather. On Titan, it rains. But not water. It rains liquid methane.
segments.headline: It rains methane

segments.text: And the rain falls in slow motion. Titan's gravity is weak, and its air is thick. So raindrops can grow much bigger than on Earth, and they drift down about six times slower, like snowflakes.
It doesn't rain often. In some places, maybe once every few years, or even centuries. But when it does, the storms can carve rivers and flood the valleys.
And those rivers flow into lakes and seas. Near Titan's north pole, the Cassini spacecraft found dozens of them, filled not with water, but with liquid methane and ethane.
segments.headline: Seas of methane

segments.text: The biggest one is called Kraken Mare. It's larger than the Caspian Sea, the largest lake on Earth.

files: PIA17655 Kraken Mare crop no labels.jpg
visual.query: PIA17655 Kraken Mare crop no labels

segments.headline: Kraken Mare

segments.text: Another sea, Ligeia Mare, is about one hundred and sixty meters deep in places. Taller than a forty-story building.
Titan holds hundreds of times more liquid hydrocarbons than all the known oil and gas on Earth.

files: PIA17655 Kraken Mare crop no labels.jpg
visual.query: PIA17655 Kraken Mare crop no labels

segments.text: So, could you go for a swim? Here's why you'd never want to.

files: PIA17655 Kraken Mare crop no labels.jpg
visual.query: PIA17655 Kraken Mare crop no labels

segments.headline: Going for a swim?

segments.text: Liquid methane is less than half as dense as water. Your body wouldn't float in it. You'd sink straight to the bottom, like a stone.
And your warm suit would be a hundred and eighty degrees warmer than the liquid. The methane touching you would boil, wrapping you in a fizzing cloud of bubbles.
segments.headline: It would boil around you

segments.text: Then the cold would win. The sea would pull the heat out of your suit far faster than air ever could. You'd freeze solid, deep under a sea of liquid gas.
And there's another hidden ocean. Deep under Titan's icy crust, scientists think there's a huge ocean of salty liquid water. Some wonder if something could live there.
segments.headline: A hidden ocean

segments.text: Now the payoff I promised. On Titan, you could fly. With your own arms.
segments.headline: Human flight

segments.text: Titan's gravity is only about one seventh of Earth's. You'd weigh about as much as a bag of groceries.

visual.label: of Earth's gravity
visual.sub: a 70 kg person weighs about 10 kg

segments.text: And the air is about four times denser than ours. So if you strapped a pair of wings to your arms and flapped, you could lift off the ground and glide over the methane seas.

files: Formation skydiving with smoke at the Wings Over Miami air show.jpg
visual.query: Formation skydiving with smoke at the Wings Over Miami air show

segments.headline: Strap on some wings

segments.text: Scientists have actually said this. Titan may be the one place in the solar system where human-powered flight would be easy.

files: Hot Air Balloon Ride by Sky Waltz.jpg
visual.query: Hot Air Balloon Ride by Sky Waltz

segments.text: So here's my question. Would you strap on a pair of wings and fly over the seas of Titan? Tell us in the comments.

visual.q: Would you strap on wings and fly on Titan?

segments.text: And a flying robot is on its way. NASA's Dragonfly is a nuclear-powered drone, about the size of a car. It's planned to launch in July 2028.
segments.headline: Dragonfly

segments.text: After a journey of about six years, it should arrive in the mid-2030s. It will hop from place to place, flying across the dunes to study the building blocks of life.
Titan is a frozen copy of Earth. Rain, rivers and seas, made from all the wrong ingredients. A beautiful place to fly over. And the very last place you'd ever want to go for a swim.
